title: The builder who asks first

beats.say: A client says, build me a house. Do you start laying bricks?
No. A good builder asks questions first. How many people will live there? What is the budget? A design interview works the same way. The prompt is short on purpose, so you must ask.
Then the builder explains each choice. Brick, because it lasts. Not wood, because of fire. They plan for trouble, like burst pipes. And they use numbers: how many rooms, how many square metres.
So interviewers score four things: asking, justifying, planning for failure, and using numbers. There is no single right house.

check.q: Why are design interview prompts kept short on purpose?
opts: To see whether you ask what is needed before building
To hide the right answer tool
check.why: A vague prompt tests whether you clarify requirements first, which is the first of the four things scored.

work: Before your next project, write three questions you must answer before choosing any tool.
Practise a one-line prompt aloud and ask five clarifying questions before drawing anything.

title: Let the numbers pick the tools

beats.say: Ten million payments a day. Is that a big system or a small one?
Do the maths aloud. A day has about eighty-six thousand seconds. Ten million divided by that is roughly one hundred fifteen events a second. Assume peak is ten times, so about twelve hundred.
If each event is one kilobyte, that is ten gigabytes a day, and about three point six terabytes a year. One modest cluster handles that. You do not need exotic tools.
So the order is: clarify, estimate, draw the boxes, justify each one, then break it on purpose. Numbers decide the tools, not the other way round.

check.q: A system gets 10 million events a day. What is the average rate per second?
check.why: 10 million divided by roughly 86,400 seconds is about 115 per second. Peak is a separate multiplier.

work: Memorise that a day is about 86 thousand seconds and a year about 30 million seconds.
For a system you run, write average rate, peak rate and daily storage on one line.

title: Why strong engineers still fail

beats.say: Why do strong engineers still fail design rounds?
Usually they name tools before asking anything. Kafka and Spark in the first minute. The interviewer hears a memorised answer, not a decision.

Second, no rejected alternative. Say why Kafka over a plain queue: replay, and many readers. Third, no failure story. If a consumer dies, it restarts from its saved position, so events may repeat. Writes must be idempotent, meaning safe to run twice.
Finally, check your numbers. Off by a thousand times, and you have picked the wrong architecture.

show.title: Sanity check
items: Is the order of magnitude right?

check.q: A consumer crashes and restarts from its last saved position. What must the sink tolerate?
check.why: Restarting from a saved position can replay events, so writes must be idempotent.

work: For each box in a past design, write one rejected alternative and why.
List what happens on component death, late data, and double volume.

title: When the boring answer wins

beats.say: Your design handles a hundred fifteen events a second. Do you really need a streaming platform?
Often not. A queue and a database can carry that load for far less money and far fewer pages at night. Complexity is a cost, paid in people and on-call hours.
So pick one design, and say what would change your mind. If volume grows a hundred times, or latency drops below a second, you move to streaming. Name that trigger aloud.
Depth beats breadth. Spend your time where the risk is, and show you can trade cost, speed and safety on purpose.

show.title: Architect habits
items: Spend time on the riskiest box

check.q: At 115 events a second with relaxed latency, what is the strongest answer?
opts: Full streaming stack for future growth
A simple queue and database, plus a stated trigger to scale
Refuse to answer without more data
check.why: Matching complexity to measured load and naming when to change shows senior judgement.

work: Add a 'we would change this if' line to every design you present.
Estimate monthly cost for the simple and the complex version of one design.

title: Why a method beats improvising

beats.say: Why do smart engineers freeze when asked to design a data system in forty-five minutes? Because they start drawing boxes before they know what they are building.

Think of building a house. First you ask the family how many people and what budget. Then you estimate the bricks. Then you sketch the floor plan. Only then do you detail the kitchen and the plumbing.
A design interview works the same way. Ask, do rough math, draw, go deep on two parts, test what breaks, then wrap up. Skipping the questions is like pouring concrete before you know the family size.

check.q: Why ask questions before drawing anything?
opts: It wastes time so the interviewer relaxes
You cannot choose a good design until you know what it must do and how big it is
Drawing is always wrong in interviews
check.why: Requirements and size decide the design. Drawing before knowing them means guessing and probably redoing the work.

work: Before your next design discussion at work, write down three questions about volume, freshness and users.
Practice sketching a pipeline only after listing what must come out of it.

title: The six steps and their minutes

beats.say: How do you spend forty-five minutes so nothing important gets missed?

Clarify for five to eight minutes: what comes in, what goes out, for whom, and how fresh, big and correct it must be. Then estimate for three to five. Fifty thousand events a second at one kilobyte is fifty megabytes a second, about four terabytes a day.

Next, draw the flow for eight to ten minutes: sources, ingest, raw storage, processing, serving, consumers. One sentence per box. Go deep on two components for ten to fifteen. Break it for five. Close in two to three.

check.q: At 50,000 events per second and 1 kilobyte each, roughly how much data arrives per day?
check.why: 50,000 times 1 kilobyte is 50 megabytes per second. Times 86,400 seconds is about 4.3 terabytes.

work: Memorize the quick conversion: megabytes per second times 86,400 gives daily volume.
Time yourself on a mock design and check you leave five minutes for breaking it.

title: Guarantees, assumptions and the break-it step

beats.say: What do senior candidates say that juniors forget? They state the guarantee out loud.

show.sub: Say it before you are asked

beats.say: For example: dashboards are at most thirty seconds behind and may revise for two minutes; the daily numbers are final. That shows you know late data exists, and when a number stops changing.

Also say your assumptions. If the interviewer stays quiet, announce: I'll assume fifty thousand events per second at peak. An unspoken guess is a hidden risk. Size for the peak, not the average, or you will undersize everything.

show.title: Say it aloud
items: Write it where they can see

beats.say: Then in the break-it step, walk each box. What if it dies? What if events arrive late, or twice? What if traffic grows ten times?

check.q: The interviewer does not answer your question about volume. What should you do?
opts: State a number as an assumption, such as 50,000 events per second at peak, and continue
check.why: Stating the assumption keeps you moving and lets the interviewer correct it. Silence or skipping hides the risk.

work: Add a one-line freshness and correctness guarantee to every pipeline design doc.
List assumed peak versus average load in your next capacity estimate.

title: Bending the method like an architect

beats.say: Is a fixed script always right for forty-five minutes? No, and an architect knows where to bend it.

show.sub: Spend time where the risk is

beats.say: Spend the depth where the risk is. If the interviewer cares about correctness, shrink the drawing and go deeper on duplicates and late data. Do not spend ten minutes on a perfect diagram of a simple batch job.

Let the numbers choose the design. Fifty megabytes a second needs only a handful of partitions, but ten times growth needs dozens. If a thirty second delay is acceptable, micro-batches may cost far less than true streaming.
Close by naming what you traded away, such as freshness for cost, and what you would build next.

show.title: Close well
items: Say what you would build next

check.q: The business accepts dashboards being 30 seconds behind. What does that allow?
opts: Cheaper micro-batch processing instead of true streaming
check.why: A relaxed freshness target lets you trade latency for lower cost and simpler operations.

work: For each pipeline you own, write the freshness target and ask if a cheaper approach would meet it.
Rehearse a closing statement that names two trade-offs and one next step.

title: The library and the front desk

beats.say: Why would a tiny question freeze your app, when it asks the company's giant data warehouse?

Picture a huge research library. One librarian can spend an hour pulling hundreds of books to answer one deep question. That is a warehouse. It is brilliant at heavy work. But now a thousand people at the door each ask, what time do you open? They queue for hours.

So you add noticeboards at the door. A phone book answers who is this customer, instantly. A live scoreboard answers how many sales this minute. A book index finds a word. Name the question first, then pick the board.

check.q: Thousands of users each ask a small question many times a second. What is the problem with sending them all to the warehouse?
opts: The warehouse cannot store that little data
It handles heavy queries well but many concurrent small ones badly
check.why: Warehouses are built for heavy analytical queries. Thousands of tiny concurrent lookups queue up and cost a lot, so a purpose-built serving store fits better.

work: List the live product features that read from your warehouse today.
For each one, write down the question it asks and how fast it must answer.

title: Key lookups: Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra

beats.say: How can one lookup come back in a millisecond when you hold a billion records?

Redis keeps data in memory, so a read takes well under a millisecond. It suits counters, sessions, and the latest value per user. DynamoDB and Cassandra use a partition key. The system hashes the key, and the hash picks the machine. So a lookup goes straight to one node and never scans.

Inside a partition, a sort key in DynamoDB, or clustering columns in Cassandra, keep rows in order. So, the last ten orders for user 42, is one ordered read. The catch is you design the table around the query. In Cassandra that means one table per query pattern.

check.q: In DynamoDB, what does the partition key do?
opts: Is hashed to decide which node holds the item
check.why: The partition key is hashed to pick the node, so a lookup goes straight there. The sort key is what orders items inside it.

work: Write the exact query your feature needs before you choose keys.
Check that your partition key has many distinct values so load spreads.

title: Live analytics and search stores

beats.say: Your dashboard has ten thousand users, each wanting a live count of the last five minutes. Which store survives that?

Pinot, Druid and ClickHouse are columnar. They store each column together, so summing one field reads only that column, not whole rows. They ingest straight from Kafka, so events are queryable within seconds. Uber uses Pinot for user-facing analytics.

Elasticsearch uses an inverted index, a map from each word to the documents holding it. That makes text search and log exploration fast. For complex SQL where seconds are fine, use the warehouse: Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery, or Trino over the lake.

show.title: Match the pattern
items: Text and logs: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch
Fresh aggregates, many users: Pinot, Druid, ClickHouse
Heavy SQL, seconds fine: the warehouse

check.q: Why does a columnar store sum one field quickly?
opts: It reads only that column, not whole rows
It keeps all data in memory only
It stores one row per node
check.why: Columnar layout keeps each column together, so an aggregate touches only the bytes it needs.

work: Identify dashboards that need fresh data for many concurrent users.
Test one such query on a columnar store and compare latency under load.

title: Where serving stores bite

beats.say: Why does a healthy DynamoDB table throttle at a fraction of its capacity?

Because the hash sends every request for one key to one partition. If a single celebrity user or one date value takes most traffic, that one partition saturates while others sit idle. Pick keys with many distinct values, or add a random suffix to spread the load.

Second gotcha. Tables fit known queries. A new question means a new table, an index, or a backfill. In Cassandra, every table holds a copy, so each write must update all of them. Third, Redis lives in memory. A crash can lose data, so treat it as rebuildable.

show.title: More gotchas
items: New query pattern means new table or backfill
Redis is memory: rebuildable, not the only copy

check.q: A table has a partition key of today's date. What is likely to happen?
opts: All current writes hit one partition and it throttles
check.why: Every write today shares one key, so one partition takes all the load while the rest idle.

work: Check your busiest partition keys for skew before launch.
Document how each Redis dataset gets rebuilt after a crash.

title: Choosing, and not over-choosing

beats.say: A team wants one store to serve everything. Why does that plan fail?

Each store optimises one access pattern. So name the pattern first: latency, request rate, freshness, and concurrency. Redis memory costs far more per gigabyte than disk, so keep only latest values, with expiry. Warehouses bill for compute, so thousands of small queries burn money and still queue.

Often the best move is to precompute. Let the stream job write finished answers into DynamoDB or Redis. Use Pinot or ClickHouse only when users slice fresh data freely. If data is small, plain Postgres may do. Cassandra scales writes but needs real operations skill.

check.q: Users only ever need a fixed set of numbers per customer, updated continuously. What is the best design?
opts: Query the warehouse on each page load
Precompute in the stream job and serve from a key-value store
check.why: The question is known, so precomputed results in a key-value store give the cheapest, fastest lookups. Ad hoc engines are needed only when users slice freely.

work: Write a one-page access-pattern table before approving any new store.
Cost out memory, compute, and operations for your top two choices.

title: The AI model is a new hire

beats.say: If you hired a brilliant new colleague, would you hand them every key on day one?
Of course not. You tell them which files they may read. You check their work. You set a time and money limit. And for big decisions, a manager signs off.
An AI model in your system is that colleague. It is one more part, with its own needs. You decide what it sees, what it can change, and how you will know when it gets something wrong.

show.title: The model is one more component

beats.say: And you keep a notebook of everything it did, so any bad answer can be explained.

check.q: Why not give a new AI feature broad access to all your data and systems from the start?
opts: It makes the model slower to answer
Like a new hire, it should earn trust, so limit what it can read and change
Models cannot read large amounts of data
check.why: Limited access and human approval for big actions reduce the damage from mistakes, just as with a new employee.

work: List what data and actions any AI feature in your team's product can reach today.
Name who approves a change the model wants to make.
Check that every AI answer can be traced back to what it did.

title: Five needs of an AI component

beats.say: The interviewer says: add an AI feature to this system. What do you say first?
Treat the model as a component with five needs. Context: what data it needs, fetched through retrieval or tools. Evaluation: a fixed test set that scores quality before and after every change.
Budgets: say three seconds and two cents per request, and a plan for going over, like a cheaper model or a fallback answer. Guardrails: read only access by default, and a person approves any change.
Observability: a trace of every request, with each model call, tool call, token count and latency. Then a bad answer can be explained, not guessed at.

check.q: A request to your AI feature gives a wrong answer. Which of the five needs lets you find out why?
check.why: A trace records each model call, tool call, tokens and latency, so you can see where the answer went wrong.

work: Write the five needs as a checklist for any AI design you discuss.
Pick a per-request latency and cost budget and name the fallback.
Build a small fixed test set before you change a prompt.

title: One agent or several?

beats.say: Would you use several agents? Usually the answer is no.
One agent with good tools is cheaper, faster, and easier to debug. There is one trace to read and one context to inspect.

Several agents earn their place when work splits into independent parts. In an outage, one agent reads logs while another reads recent code changes. They run at the same time, each with a clean context.
An orchestrator then combines their findings. But every agent adds tokens, delay, and places for errors to hide. So prove the split wins on your evaluation set.

show.title: Each agent has a price
items: Prove it on your evaluation set

check.q: Which task is the best candidate for several agents?
opts: Three steps where each needs the previous answer
Reading logs and reading recent code changes during an outage
A simple question answered from one document
check.why: The two reads are independent, so they can run in parallel with separate contexts and be combined afterwards.

work: Start every design with one agent and good tools.
Split only when subtasks are truly independent.
Compare single and multi agent on the same evaluation set.

title: Reading code an assistant wrote

beats.say: An assistant wrote a working pipeline in two minutes. So what is wrong with it?

The code runs. The flaws show up over time. In one published example, it overwrote the full history on every run, re-scored records that had not changed, and averaged all of history when the business wanted a recent window.

show.title: Flaws that appear over time
items: Averages all history, not a recent window

beats.say: So ask: what happens on the second run, and the hundredth? Does it process only what changed? Does it compute what the business asked for, at the right grain and window?
Then: what does each run cost as data grows? And what happens with duplicates, late data and nulls?

show.title: Two more checks
items: Cost per run as data grows

check.q: A generated pipeline passes on its first run. What is the best next review question?
opts: Does it use my favourite library?
What happens on the second and hundredth run?
How fast did the assistant write it?
check.why: Generated code usually runs once. The real flaws are in repeat behaviour: overwrites, duplicates and reprocessing.

work: Run any generated pipeline twice and compare the output.
Check that it filters to new or changed rows only.
Test it with duplicate, late and null records.

title: The pipeline whose bill doubles

beats.say: Why does a pipeline that works today become a bill problem next year?
Say it holds ten million reviews, and a hundred thousand arrive each day. A full rewrite re-scores all ten million every night, paying for the model on records that never changed.
Next year it is twenty million, and the bill doubles, though the real work is the same hundred thousand.
The fix is incremental: score only new or changed rows, keep a stable key so reruns do not duplicate, and compute the average over a recent window, like the last thirty days.

show.title: The fix
items: Score only new or changed rows
Stable key so reruns do not duplicate

check.q: A nightly job re-scores all history with a paid model. What is the best fix?
opts: Score only new or changed rows, using a stable key
Run the job less often and accept stale data
check.why: Incremental processing makes cost follow the amount of change, not the size of history, and a stable key keeps reruns safe.

work: Find any job that rewrites or re-scores everything each run.
Add a stable key and a changed-since filter.
Define the window the business actually wants.

title: When to refuse the multi-agent design

beats.say: When would you refuse to split one agent into five?
When steps depend on each other. If step two needs step one's answer, parallel agents just wait, and you pay to pass context between them.
Cost grows too. Five agents can mean five times the tokens, and the slowest one sets your latency. Errors compound: if each is right nine times in ten, a chain of five is right about six in ten.

show.title: Chance a chain is fully right

beats.say: So start with one agent, measure on your evaluation set, and split only when the gain in quality or speed beats the cost. Keep a person approving any write.

show.title: Architect's rule
items: Split only if the gain beats the cost

check.q: Five chained agents are each right 90 percent of the time. Roughly how often is the whole chain right?
opts: About 50 percent exactly, regardless of accuracy
check.why: Probabilities multiply along a chain: 0.9 five times is about 0.59, so errors compound with each extra agent.

work: Draw your task as a dependency graph and split only independent branches.
Estimate tokens and latency for single versus multi agent designs.
Require evaluation results before approving a multi-agent design.

title: The cut phone line

beats.say: What should a bank branch do when its phone line to head office is cut?
Two branches share one ledger. The line goes down, so neither sees the other's changes. This cut is called a partition.
Option one: refuse withdrawals until the line returns. Every balance is correct, but some customers are turned away. That is choosing consistency.
Option two: keep serving, using the last balance you know. Nobody waits, but a number might be stale. That is choosing availability.
You only have to choose during the cut. When the line works, you get both.

check.q: A store keeps answering during a network partition, even though some answers may be stale. What did it choose?
check.why: Answering with possibly stale data during a partition is the availability choice. Refusing requests would be the consistency choice.

work: For each data store you own, write down whether it refuses or answers stale during a partition.
Ask which of your user actions can tolerate a stale answer and which cannot.

title: Why a crowd crushes a recovering server

beats.say: Why does a shop that reopens after a power cut sometimes get crushed again within seconds?
Everyone who was waiting rushes in at the same moment. A server that just recovered is fragile, and thousands of clients retrying together can knock it flat again.
The fix is polite waiting. After each failure, wait longer: one second, then two, then four. That is exponential backoff, meaning the wait doubles.
Add jitter, which means randomness. Each client waits a slightly different time, so the crowd trickles in instead of arriving as one wave.

check.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
opts: So clients do not all retry at the same instant
So the server can ignore duplicates
check.why: Without randomness, clients that failed together keep retrying in sync. Jitter spreads them out.

work: Check what wait time your clients use between retries.
Add randomness to any fixed retry delay.

title: Quorums with real numbers

beats.say: Three copies of your data, and one is down. How can a read still be right?
Say N is three replicas. A write waits for W copies to confirm; set W to two. A read asks R copies; set R to two.
Any two groups of two out of three must share at least one copy. So the read always touches a replica holding the latest write.
The rule is that R plus W must be bigger than N. Here two plus two is four, bigger than three.
Want faster reads? Set R to one and W to three. Reads are quick, but every write needs all replicas.

check.q: With N=5 replicas and W=3, what is the smallest R that guarantees overlap?
check.why: R + W must exceed N. With W=3 and N=5, R must be greater than 2, so R=3. Option 2 gives 2+3=5, which is not greater than 5.

work: Write down N, R and W for your main replicated store.
Check whether it can serve reads when one replica is down.

title: Why a ring beats mod N

beats.say: You add a fourth server to a cluster of three. Should most of your data move?
With simple hashing, the server is the key's hash mod the node count. Change three to four and about three quarters of keys land somewhere new. That is a huge reshuffle.
Consistent hashing puts servers and keys on a ring. Each key belongs to the next server clockwise.

chip.text: Key goes to next node clockwise

beats.say: Add a server and it takes over only the slice just before it. With four nodes, roughly one quarter of keys move.
Hash partitioning spreads load evenly but makes range scans hit every node. Range partitioning keeps neighbours together, but a hot range can overload one node.

show.title: Partitioning trade
items: Hash: even load, costly range scans

check.q: Why is consistent hashing preferred over hash mod N when nodes are added?
opts: Only a small share of keys move
It removes the need for replicas
check.why: On a ring, a new node only takes over a slice of one neighbour's keys. Mod N changes the owner of most keys.

work: Find out how your store assigns keys to nodes.
Estimate how much data would move if you added one node.

title: Retry storms and how to stop them

beats.say: Your service dies at noon and recovers at one minute past. Why does it die again?
Ten thousand clients failed, waited a fixed second, and retried together. Each wave arrives in sync, so load spikes instead of spreading.
Backoff alone does not fix it. If everyone doubles together, they still collide at one, two, four seconds. Jitter breaks the sync, by picking a random wait up to the current cap.

show.title: Backoff needs jitter
items: Jitter: random wait up to the cap

beats.say: Also cap the retries and the maximum wait, or a long outage multiplies traffic. And retry only safe calls: a repeated payment needs an idempotency key, so it applies once.

check.q: Clients use exponential backoff with no jitter. What problem remains?
opts: Clients that failed together still retry together
check.why: Identical doubling keeps clients synchronized, so spikes recur at each step. Randomness breaks the synchronization.

work: Audit retry code for caps on attempts and total wait.
Confirm that retried write calls carry an idempotency key.

title: What quorums and CAP do not promise

beats.say: If R plus W exceeds N, are reads guaranteed correct? Not quite.
Overlap only promises that one replica you read has the newest copy. The client must still pick it, usually by timestamp or version. Clock skew can pick the wrong one.
Sloppy quorums, which write to stand-in nodes during failures, break the overlap until hints are handed back. A write that fails halfway can also leave partial copies that later reads see.
And CAP is about partitions only. Without one, the real trade is latency against consistency: waiting for more replicas is slower.

show.sub: More replicas waited on, slower answer

check.q: Which situation can break the guarantee that R + W > N reads see the latest write?
opts: A sloppy quorum writing to stand-in nodes
check.why: Stand-in nodes mean the write may not sit on the replicas the read later asks, so the overlap argument no longer holds.

work: Find out if your store uses sloppy quorums or hinted handoff.
Check how it resolves conflicting versions on reads.

title: Region failure: RPO and RTO

beats.say: A whole region goes dark. What two numbers does your design owe the business?
RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data you can lose, measured in time. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long you can be down.

show.title: Two targets
items: RPO: data you can lose, in time

beats.say: Asynchronous replication to another region gives an RPO of seconds and keeps writes fast. Synchronous replication gives an RPO of zero, but every write pays cross-region latency.
RTO depends on the standby. Restoring backups takes hours, a warm standby minutes, active-active near zero, at roughly double the cost.
Pick targets from the business cost of loss, then buy only that.

show.text: Price the loss, then buy the target

check.q: The business says losing even one committed transaction on region failure is unacceptable. What does that set?
check.why: RPO measures data loss in time. No loss means RPO zero, which generally requires synchronous replication across regions.

work: Write RPO and RTO into the design doc for every critical system.
Test a failover and record the real recovery time.

title: Choosing stale or strict on purpose

beats.say: When would you choose a store that may serve stale data on purpose?
When being up matters more than being exact: shopping carts, feeds, sensor events. Use Cassandra or DynamoDB, with quorum reads for the requests that need them.
When money or inventory must be exact, choose a single-leader relational database. Refusing a request in a partition is cheaper than double-selling a seat.
The partition key matters too. Hash for even load and point lookups. Range if reports scan time windows, but split the hot recent range.
Tune per request, not per company.

check.q: Which workload is the best fit for a single-leader relational database rather than an availability-first store?
check.why: Limited inventory must not be double-sold, so refusing during a partition is better than serving stale data.

work: Classify each data domain as must-be-exact or can-be-stale.
Choose partition keys by checking real query patterns and hot-spot risk.

title: Quick count, final count

beats.say: Why does a news channel show a quick vote count tonight, then a different final count days later?

show.sub: Both are real. They answer different needs.

beats.say: Because fast and exact pull apart. The quick count uses the first reports. It is ready in minutes, but it can be slightly wrong.
The final count waits for every ballot box, and checks each one. It is slow, but you can trust it.
Data systems copy this. Every event goes down two lanes. A fast lane feeds live screens. A slow lane keeps everything and fixes mistakes later. Designing means choosing which numbers need which lane.

check.q: Why do data systems often run both a fast lane and a slow lane?
opts: Fast results are never wrong, so the slow lane is a backup
Fast gives early answers; slow gives complete, corrected answers
Two lanes are always cheaper than one
Slow lanes are only for storage, never for numbers
check.why: The fast lane trades exactness for freshness. The slow lane waits for all data and corrects mistakes, so you get both an early view and a trustworthy final one.

work: List your key dashboards and mark each one as needing a quick count or a final count.
Ask stakeholders how wrong a live number may be before it misleads them.

title: Clickstream: 30 seconds and daily

beats.say: A user clicks buy. How does that click reach a dashboard within thirty seconds, and also a daily report?

show.sub: Two freshness targets, one event stream

beats.say: The app sends the event to an ingestion service, which writes to Kafka, keyed by session. Keying keeps one session's clicks in order, in one partition.
A stream processor drops duplicates using the event id, groups clicks into sessions, and counts per minute. Those counts go to Pinot, a store built for fast dashboard queries.

Meanwhile raw events land untouched in an Iceberg bronze table. Each night, batch jobs build silver and gold, and merge late events inside a lookback window. If the stream job crashes, replay from Kafka. Idempotent sinks make the replay safe.

chip.text: Replay is safe if sinks are idempotent

check.q: The stream job crashes and you replay an hour of events from Kafka. What makes this safe?
opts: Kafka deletes events once they are read
Idempotent sinks, so repeated writes give the same result
check.why: Replay means some events are processed again. Idempotent sinks, plus dedupe on event id, mean the repeat does not double count.

work: Check whether your streaming sink can be written twice without double counting.
Define the lookback window for late data and write it down.

title: Fraud scoring in 100 milliseconds

beats.say: A card payment arrives. You have about one hundred milliseconds to decide if it is fraud. How?

The payment calls a scoring service. The service cannot compute history on the spot, so it reads precomputed features: transactions on this card in the last ten minutes, and distance from the last location.
A stream processor keeps those features fresh in a low-latency store. The model gives a score, and simple rules handle the obvious cases.
If scoring times out, a fallback rule decides, because payments must not wait. Every decision and feature value is logged to the lake, for training and audit.

check.q: Why does the scoring service read precomputed features instead of calculating them per payment?
opts: Computing history on the spot would blow the latency budget
check.why: Aggregating ten minutes of history per request is too slow for a 100 ms budget. A stream job computes it ahead, so scoring is a quick lookup.

work: Write the latency budget and split it across each call in your scoring path.
Log the exact feature values used for every decision so you can reproduce training data.

title: City speed from noisy pings

beats.say: Average speed of every car in a city, live. Why is that harder than averaging a column?

show.sub: One ping alone has no speed

beats.say: Speed needs two pings from the same driver. So the stream job keeps state per driver: the last position and time. Kafka is keyed by driver so one worker sees all of that driver's pings.

chip.text: Key by driver for local state

beats.say: Phones are messy. Pings arrive out of order, so you use event time and a watermark, which is how long you wait for stragglers. GPS jumps give impossible speeds, so discard them.
Then group by hexagonal cell or city in sliding windows. Write volume is huge, so the raw pings go to the lake and only small aggregates go to the dashboard store.

check.q: Why key the ping stream by driver?
opts: So one worker holds each driver's previous ping to compute speed
To spread load evenly across cities
To make pings arrive in order globally
check.why: Speed comes from consecutive pings. Keying by driver sends them to the same worker, which keeps the last position as local state.

work: Add a plausibility filter, such as a maximum speed, before aggregating.
Decide the watermark by measuring how late real pings actually arrive.

title: IoT: late, skewed, expensive

beats.say: A device reconnects after two hours offline and uploads seven thousand two hundred readings at once. What breaks?

show.sub: One per second, two hours offline

beats.say: Device clocks drift, so you trust event time with a skew check, not arrival time. Late readings need a watermark, and a path to correct old windows.
Storage cost is the quiet danger. One message per second per device is eighty-six thousand four hundred rows a day. Keep full resolution for thirty days, then minute averages.
Alerts have a trap too. A noisy rule pages people all night, and they start ignoring it. Alert on sustained anomalies, not single spikes, and dedupe repeats.

show.title: Avoid alert fatigue
items: Alert on sustained anomalies, not one spike
Dedupe repeats from the same device
Route by severity so pages stay rare

check.q: A device uploads old readings after reconnecting. Which time should windows use?
opts: Event time, with a watermark and a skew check
check.why: Arrival time puts old readings in the wrong window. Event time is right, but device clocks drift, so check skew and allow late corrections.

work: Compare device timestamps with arrival times and flag large gaps.
Set tiered retention: full resolution for 30 days, minute averages beyond.

title: Fail open or fail closed

beats.say: Your scoring service is down. Do you approve every payment, or decline every payment?

That is fail-open versus fail-closed, and it is a business choice. Fail-open risks fraud losses. Fail-closed loses sales and angers honest customers. Many teams fail open for small amounts and closed for large ones.
Streaming features cost more to run than batch. Only stream what needs it, like card velocity. Home country can be a daily batch feature.
Remember the feedback loop. Chargebacks arrive weeks later, so labels are late and your newest model is trained blind on recent fraud. Plan for that delay.

show.title: Late labels
items: Recent fraud is missing from training data
Backfill labels and retrain on a delay

check.q: Which statement about streaming features is most sound?
opts: Stream every feature for best accuracy
Stream only features whose value decays fast; batch the rest
check.why: Streaming adds cost and complexity. Fast-decaying signals like card velocity need it. Slow facts such as home country work fine from daily batch.

work: Get the business to sign off on fail-open or fail-closed, by transaction amount.
Tag each feature as stream or batch and justify any stream choice with money saved.

title: Metrics: consistency beats speed

beats.say: Two executives show different numbers for completed trips. Faster dashboards will not fix that. What will?

show.sub: A trust problem, not a speed problem

beats.say: The problem is consistency, not speed. Define each metric once, in a semantic layer, so every dashboard computes completed trips the same way.
Pre-aggregate daily and weekly tables so queries are quick, and have them ready by seven in the morning. Certify core metrics with tests and a named owner.

show.title: Make it dependable
items: Certified metrics with tests and owners

beats.say: Reconcile with finance, and restrict access by role. Do not build this for a small team with one dashboard. The cost of governance beats the gain.

show.title: Trade-offs
items: Skip it for one team and one dashboard

check.q: Two dashboards disagree on completed trips. What is the best structural fix?
opts: Define the metric once in a semantic layer both use
check.why: Disagreement comes from separate definitions. One governed definition, with an owner and tests, makes every consumer compute it identically.

work: Pick your top five metrics and name an owner for each.
Write a test that reconciles a core metric against finance totals.

title: Log platform: where cost hides

beats.say: A log platform takes in terabytes a day. Where does the money actually go?
Agents like Fluent Bit ship logs to Kafka. A stream job parses them, masks sensitive fields at ingest, and writes Iceberg tables by day and service.
Streams create tiny files, and tiny files slow every query. Compact hourly. Cost scales per gigabyte, so set retention per service and drop noisy debug logs early.
If you mostly need free-text search, a log search engine fits better. Trino over Iceberg suits analysis at lower cost. Restrict security logs by role.

show.title: Pick the right engine
items: Analysis at low cost: Trino over Iceberg

check.q: Why compact Iceberg log tables hourly?
opts: Streaming writes make many tiny files that slow queries
check.why: Frequent small writes create many tiny files. Each file adds overhead to planning and reads, so merging them keeps queries fast and cheap.

work: Measure file counts and average file size in your busiest log table.
Set a retention period per service and review the biggest log producers for noise.

title: Counting cars before building the bridge

beats.say: How do you know a bridge is wide enough before you build it? You count the cars.
Data works the same way. Picture a pizza shop that sells 86,400 slices a day. A day has 86,400 seconds. So that is about one slice every second.
But dinner rush is busier than the average. Plan for two or three times as many orders, or the queue spills into the street.

Next, how big is each box, and how long do you keep the boxes? Orders per second, times box size, times days kept, tells you how much storage room to rent. That is capacity arithmetic. A few numbers you remember, then multiplication.

check.q: Why plan for two or three times the average rate?
opts: Averages are always wrong by that much
Busy periods bunch up and the average hides them
check.why: Load is uneven. The system must survive the busiest moments, not the mean.

work: Take one pipeline you own and write its events per second, average and peak.
Learn that a day is about 100 thousand seconds, so a million a day is about 12 per second.

title: From trips to terabytes

beats.say: Is 100 million events a day a lot? Not really. It is about 1,200 per second.
Start with one number. A day has 86,400 seconds, call it 100 thousand. So 1 million events a day is about 12 per second, and 1 billion is about 11,600.

show.title: Memorise these
items: 86,400 seconds a day, about 10 to the 5
1 million a day is about 12 per second
1 billion a day is about 11,600 per second

beats.say: Meridian has 2 million trips a day, each emitting 50 events. That is 100 million events a day. Peak runs two to three times average, so plan for 3,000 to 4,000 per second.

At 1 kilobyte each, that is 100 gigabytes a day, about 36 terabytes a year. Parquet is five to ten times smaller, so roughly 5 terabytes. If one consumer handles 5,000 per second, a dozen partitions cover peak.

check.q: 2 million trips a day, 50 events each. Roughly what is the average events per second?
check.why: 100 million events divided by about 86,400 seconds is roughly 1,200 per second.

work: Work out events per second, peak, and yearly bytes for one dataset you own.
Write the result as a one-line sizing note in the design doc.

title: Where the estimate breaks

beats.say: Your estimate says 1,200 events per second. So why did the pipeline fall over at noon?
Because average hides peaks. Trips bunch up at rush hour, and a retry storm or a replay of old data can multiply load again. Size for peak, two to three times average, not the mean.

Second gotcha: sizes. A one kilobyte JSON event is a guess. Measure real payloads, because a few fat events skew everything. Also remember replication: with three copies, 100 gigabytes a day really stores 300.

show.title: Size traps
items: 1 KB per event is a guess, so sample real payloads
A few fat events skew the average
Three replicas turn 100 GB into 300 GB

beats.say: Third: Parquet's five to ten times is typical, not promised. Random ids compress badly. Test on a sample before you quote it.

check.q: Which input most likely makes a capacity estimate too low?
opts: Ignoring replication and retry or replay load
Rounding a day to 100 thousand seconds
check.why: Replicas multiply stored bytes and retries or replays multiply rate. Rounding seconds is harmless.

work: Sample real events to get actual average size instead of assuming 1 KB.
Multiply storage by the replication factor before quoting a number.
Test Parquet compression on one real day of data.

title: Does the arithmetic justify the design?

beats.say: At 3,000 events per second, why would you pick Kafka at all?
A single database could take 3,000 writes a second. So the arithmetic alone does not justify Kafka. It tells you the question to answer.

Justify it with other reasons. Several consumers need the same stream. You want replay after a bug. Bursts must not overload the database. Those reasons, not volume, earn the extra cost of running a cluster.

show.title: Real reasons for Kafka
items: Many consumers read the same stream

beats.say: Then show the cost. Storing 36 terabytes of raw JSON costs far more than 5 terabytes of Parquet. Twelve partitions with headroom is a small cluster. If load grew a hundred times, you would redesign. Say where your design breaks.

check.q: Peak load is 3,500 events per second. What best justifies adding Kafka?
opts: 3,500 per second is too much for any database
Several consumers need the stream and you need replay
Kafka is always cheaper than a database
check.why: At this rate volume alone does not require Kafka. Fan-out, replay and burst buffering are the real reasons.

work: In every design, write the rate number next to each component you add and say why it is needed.
State the load multiple at which your design would need to change.
